title: Berkshire 2016 letter: float, repurchases, adjusted earnings, and the hedge-fund bet
summary: Buffett explains why book value understates Berkshire's intrinsic value, how to judge buybacks by price versus value, how insurance float works, why "adjusted earnings" mislead, and why low-cost index funds beat high-fee managers. He also owns up to his Dexter Shoe and General Re mistakes.

principles.text: Buybacks only help continuing shareholders when shares are bought below intrinsic value; the result depends entirely on the price paid.
principles.quote: the question of whether a repurchase action is value-enhancing or value-destroying for continuing shareholders is entirely purchase-price dependent.

principles.text: Float is best seen as a revolving fund, not a typical liability; if it is costless and long-enduring, its true cost is far below its accounting liability.
principles.quote: But to think of float as a typical liability is a major mistake. It should instead be viewed as a revolving fund.

principles.text: A sound insurer needs four disciplines, the last being willingness to walk away when the right premium isn't available.
principles.quote: (4) be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can’t be obtained.

principles.text: Widespread fear is the investor's friend because it creates bargains; personal fear is the enemy and unwarranted.
principles.quote: First, widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases. Second, personal fear is your enemy.

principles.text: Active investors in aggregate must trail passive ones after costs, so most investors should hold low-cost index funds.
principles.quote: Both large and small investors should stick with low-cost index funds.

principles.text: Treating stock-based compensation or recurring restructuring as non-costs is misleading, and chasing 'adjusted earnings' breeds a bad culture.
principles.quote: bad behavior is contagious: CEOs who overtly look for ways to report high numbers tend to foster a culture in which subordinates strive to be “helpful” as well.
